analysis.one_liner: Ends the auto insurance industry's exemption from federal antitrust laws for rate-setting.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it died in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted the insurance industry from federal antitrust laws, allowing insurers to share pricing information and coordinate rates without facing antitrust scrutiny. This bill would have removed that shield for personal auto insurance only. Insurers could still share loss statistics and pure premium data, but they could no longer jointly develop or distribute manuals containing a final rate — the price consumers actually pay. Violations would be subject to the Sherman Act, Clayton Act, and FTC Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers who buy personal auto insurance. The bill's stated purpose was to promote competition in auto insurance, on the theory that coordinated rate-setting among insurers keeps prices higher than a competitive market would produce. Competition under antitrust law would push insurers to compete on price rather than follow industry-agreed rate manuals.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends McCarran-Ferguson so that antitrust laws apply to personal motor vehicle insurance conduct, ending the industry's broad exemption in that line of business [S3].

The bill states Congress's findings that the insurance industry's broad antitrust exemption has adversely affected free competition in personal motor vehicle insurance, and that its purpose is to protect consumers by promoting competition [S3].
Insurers could no longer jointly prepare and distribute rating manuals containing a final rate, or guidelines regarding a final rate — the coordination mechanism the bill targets [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Auto insurance companies, which would lose the ability to coordinate rate-setting through shared final-rate manuals and would face antitrust liability for collusive pricing. Industry advisory organizations that publish rate manuals would have to stop including final rates. The bill preserved the industry's ability to share statistical data, pure premium figures, and fraud information, so the burden falls on coordinated pricing, not on the data infrastructure itself.

drawbacks.text: The bill carved out a long list of permitted joint activities — collecting and sharing loss data, statistical plans, pure premium rate data, policy forms, fraud information — which insurers and rating organizations argued were necessary for small insurers to price accurately; critics of antitrust exposure contend that shared data lowers, not raises, prices by letting small carriers compete with large ones [S3].

The exemption the bill targeted was limited: the industry could still rely on state regulation and approval of rates, so repealing the federal exemption shifts enforcement to antitrust litigation, which can be costly and slow compared with state rate regulation [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real but bounded. The bill was drafted narrowly: it left the exemption intact for every other line of insurance, and it carefully preserved the statistical and data-sharing functions that support accurate pricing, going after only the joint setting and distribution of final rates. The genuine objection is that shared ratemaking data helps small insurers compete, and antitrust lawsuits can be a blunt instrument compared with state regulation. But the bill's design shows awareness of that risk — it allowed pure premium data sharing while banning shared final rates — making the bill a measured competition measure rather than a sweeping attack on industry practice.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Economic and Commercial Law subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Jim Courter introduced the bill on February 28, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
On March 27, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law, where it remained with no further action through the end of the 101st Congress in January 1991 [S5].
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Auto insurers and their rating organizations. Because the bill died in committee without a hearing, vote, or cosponsor, they kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for coordinated rate-setting in personal auto insurance, and drivers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Auto insurers, who kept their antitrust exemption

for.name: Jim Courter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the antitrust exemption from personal auto insurance; it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and never reported it out or held any action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Insurance industry
against.role: Auto insurers and rating organizations benefiting from the McCarran-Ferguson exemption
against.what_they_did: The industry benefited from the exemption the bill targeted; no insurer supported the measure, which drew no cosponsors from either party.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a cosponsor from either party, so support was a single Republican member with no bloc on either side to measure.

industries.note: The bill would have made antitrust laws apply to personal auto insurance, barring insurers from jointly preparing and distributing rating manuals containing final rates. Coordinated rate-setting is a mechanism that can keep prices above competitive levels, and consumers pay those premiums.

Rating organizations compile and publish the rate manuals the industry uses. The bill preserved their statistical, data-collection, and pure-premium functions but prohibited them from distributing manuals containing a final rate, changing their core product in personal auto lines.
